raw_case_text:
A 21-year-old G2P1 cisgender woman at 16 weeks and 5 days of gestation with a history of uncontrolled congenital HIV and recently diagnosed disseminated cryptococcosis (diagnosed at 9 weeks of gestation) presented to our institution with left-sided headache and photophobia concerning for relapsed cryptococcal disease. Laboratory evaluation revealed a CD4+ count of 9 cells/mm3 and an HIV-1 RNA viral load of 31,600 copies/mL. Several weeks prior, she was started on single-agent L-AmB 4 mg/kg once daily induction therapy; however, this was terminated prematurely due to worsening renal function and gastrointestinal intolerance. At 13 weeks and 5 days of gestation, she began treatment with oral fluconazole 400 mg daily and antiretroviral therapy (ART) with bictegravir, tenofovir alafenamide, and emtricitabine, which had initially been delayed due to concerns for immune reconstitution inflammatory syndrome (IRIS).
Although she verbalized compliance with fluconazole and ART, she was experiencing a lot of nausea and vomiting in the setting of pregnancy, raising concerns for suboptimal absorption. L-AmB and intravenous fluconazole 800 mg daily were started after admission. Within minutes of starting L-AmB, the patient became tachycardic, tachypneic, and hypoxemic. L-AmB was discontinued, and she received antihistamines and supplemental oxygen with rapid symptom improvement. L-AmB was held indefinitely, and she continued fluconazole. After discussion with the Maternal-Fetal Medicine team, flucytosine 25 mg/kg every 6 h was added as the benefits of treatment were deemed to outweigh the risks of teratogenicity in the second trimester. Blood cultures returned positive for C. neoformans (Fig. 1).
We consulted Allergy/Immunology regarding desensitization to L-AmB or an alternative amphotericin formulation, but given the severity of her prior reaction, desensitization to any formulation was deemed too risky. The decision was made to continue flucytosine and fluconazole. She improved, and after approximately 3 weeks of hospitalization, she left against medical advice. It is unclear if she continued taking her medications as an outpatient.
Over the next few weeks, she was readmitted multiple times for persistent symptoms, with workup revealing a low CD4+ count and increased HIV viral load, suggesting suboptimal medication adherence. Her blood and cerebral spinal fluid (CSF) cultures remained positive for C. neoformans (Fig. 1, Table 1). As her condition progressed, concerns arose about inadequate flucytosine levels due to persistent nausea and vomiting, prompting us to proceed with amphotericin B lipid complex (Amb-LC) 5 mg/kg once daily desensitization (Fig. 1). The patient was admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) for a 10-step desensitization protocol, which she tolerated (Table 2). She continued treatment with Amb-LC and flucytosine. Thirty-four days after desensitization, she developed facial swelling and erythema, which improved with diphenhydramine and cessation of the Amb-LC infusion. She tolerated subsequent doses of Amb-LC without any additional reactions.
CSF cultures remained positive for C. neoformans, prompting fluconazole addition to her regimen (Fig. 1). She developed severe pre-eclampsia, received peripartum zidovudine, and underwent cesarean delivery at 33 weeks and 3 days. The baby required a brief stay in the neonatal intensive care unit after birth but was otherwise healthy. Her CSF cultures cleared a few weeks after her delivery (Fig. 1). Amb-LC was discontinued 2 weeks later, and she was discharged on flucytosine and fluconazole.
Approximately 5 months later, she returned to the hospital with relapsed cryptococcal meningitis. Amb-LC was unavailable at that time, so she underwent a 12-step L-AmB desensitization without incident (Tables 3 and 4). She was initially treated with L-AmB and flucytosine; however, due to persistently positive CSF cultures and the observation that the minimum inhibitory concentration (MIC) of amphotericin for the C. neoformans isolate increased from 1 microg/mL during her first admission to 4 microg/mL at her fourth admission, fluconazole was added to the regimen (Fig. 1, Table 5). Approximately 6 weeks into her antifungal treatment course, and nearly 1 month after starting treatment with L-AmB, flucytosine, and fluconazole, she developed a sudden change in her mental status, and an MRI brain revealed new leptomeningeal enhancement suggestive of IRIS. CSF culture at this time was negative (Fig. 1). ART was briefly held, and she was placed on a steroid taper with clinical improvement. She was discharged after approximately 2 months of hospitalization with maintenance fluconazole therapy for at least 1 year until viral suppression and a CD4+ count >=100 cells/mm3 were achieved. Due to past issues with adherence to oral ART, we administered one dose of injectable cabotegravir-rilpivirine prior to discharge. She has continued on this treatment since discharge, and 2.5 years later, at the time of writing, maintains an undetectable viral load with a recent CD4+ count of 391 cells/mm3. Her infant remained negative for HIV at 1 year of age.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 21-year-old pregnant woman (G2P1 at 16 weeks and 5 days of gestation) with congenital HIV and recently diagnosed disseminated cryptococcosis presented with left-sided headache and photophobia.
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient, who had uncontrolled congenital HIV and disseminated cryptococcosis diagnosed at 9 weeks of gestation (previously intolerant of liposomal amphotericin B due to nephrotoxicity and GI upset, and started on oral fluconazole 400 mg/day and bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine at 13 weeks and 5 days of gestation), presented at 16 weeks and 5 days with left-sided headache, photophobia, and pregnancy-related nausea and vomiting impairing oral medication absorption.
subjective.past_medical_history: Uncontrolled congenital HIV infection, current pregnancy (G2P1, 16w5d gestation), and disseminated cryptococcosis diagnosed at 9 weeks of gestation.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for left-sided headache, photophobia, nausea, and vomiting. Home medications: fluconazole 400 mg daily and bictegravir/tenofovir alafenamide/emtricitabine.

objective.physical_examination: Developed acute tachycardia, tachypnea, and hypoxemia within minutes of starting liposomal amphotericin B infusion on admission; later developed facial swelling and erythema 34 days after amphotericin B lipid complex desensitization, severe pre-eclampsia at 33 weeks of gestation, and acute altered mental status during a subsequent postpartum readmission.
objective.routine_investigations: HIV-1 RNA viral load was 31,600 copies/mL on initial presentation. Blood cultures were persistently positive for Cryptococcus neoformans across multiple admissions.
objective.advanced_workup: Initial CD4+ count was 9 cells/mm3. Serial lumbar punctures yielded CSF cultures persistently positive for Cryptococcus neoformans (with amphotericin B MIC rising from 1 ug/mL on first admission to 4 ug/mL on fourth admission). During her fourth admission (5 months postpartum), brain MRI showed new leptomeningeal enhancement with negative CSF cultures.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Final diagnosis of refractory/relapsing HIV-associated disseminated cryptococcosis and cryptococcal meningitis in pregnancy complicated by amphotericin B anaphylaxis/hypersensitivity and postpartum CNS IRIS, confirmed by serial positive blood and CSF cultures for Cryptococcus neoformans. Following acute anaphylactoid reaction to L-AmB, she was treated with IV fluconazole (800 mg/day) and oral flucytosine (25 mg/kg every 6 hours), and upon readmission underwent a 10-step ICU desensitization to amphotericin B lipid complex (Amb-LC 5 mg/kg/day) plus flucytosine and fluconazole, delivering a healthy HIV-negative infant via cesarean section at 33w3d for severe pre-eclampsia (with peripartum zidovudine) before CSF sterilization. Five months postpartum, relapsed CM with elevated amphotericin MIC (4 ug/mL) was treated via 12-step L-AmB desensitization plus flucytosine and fluconazole; subsequent culture-negative CNS IRIS responded to a corticosteroid taper, and transition to injectable cabotegravir-rilpivirine and maintenance fluconazole achieved sustained viral suppression and CD4 recovery (391 cells/mm3) at 2.5 years.
